cur:manuscripts-drogo-temptation.summary: Around and within the initial D, Christ appears three times, haloed and in a green mantle, as a shaggy, horned devil confronts him: on the ground with the devil pointing to stones, standing high on the upright of the letter, and on the pinnacle of the Temple at the right, where the devil urges him to cast himself down. Above, angels fly in to minister to him. The scene illustrates the prayers for the first Sunday of Lent.
facts: The Drogo Sacramentary was written and painted for the personal use of Drogo, Bishop of Metz and a son of Charlemagne; it contains only the prayers spoken by the bishop at Mass through the year.
Its scenes are set inside the initial letters of the prayers, in delicate gold vine-scrolls — an early and influential use of the historiated initial.
cur:manuscripts-drogo-temptation.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file; the miniature is an initial within the text page.

cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-crucifixio.summary: Against a deep blue ground, Christ hangs on a tall cross with arms outstretched beneath a titulus, between the two thieves on their crosses, who are labelled Gestas and Dismas; Longinus pierces his side with a spear while Stephaton raises the sponge, and angels with censers hover at the top beside the darkened sun and moon. At the foot of the cross, the base rests on a stepped structure with a small figure, suggesting the tomb of Adam beneath Golgotha.
facts: Unlike most Beatus manuscripts, the Girona copy opens with a cycle of pictures of the life and Passion of Christ before the commentary on the Apocalypse.

The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-crucifixio.notes: The figure at the foot of the cross is small and not certainly identifiable in the available image.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: A haloed figure in a purple mantle falls headlong through the air from the edge of a great hill, where men with clubs stand at the top, while a group watches from the left. The verse above reads 'though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the Lord upholdeth him with his hand'. The scene probably shows the attempt of the people of Nazareth to throw Christ from the brow of their hill.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The identification with Luke 4:29 is a probable interpretation, not confirmed by an inscription.
